'''Joan Sylvia Lyttle Birman''' (born May 30, 1927, in New York City)<ref name=LRiddleBio>Larry Riddle. "[https://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/birman.htm Joan S. Birman]", ''Biographies of Women Mathematicians'', at [[Agnes Scott College]]</ref> is an American mathematician, specializing in [[low-dimensional topology]]. She has made contributions to the study of [[Knot theory|knots]], [[3-manifold]]s, [[Mapping class group of a surface|mapping class groups]] of surfaces, [[geometric group theory]], [[Contact geometry|contact structures]] and [[dynamical system]]s. Birman is research professor emerita at [[Barnard College]], [[Columbia University]],<ref>{{Cite web|title=Home Page for Joan S. Birman|url=http://www.math.columbia.edu/~jb/|access-date=2020-11-06|website=www.math.columbia.edu}}</ref> where she has been since 1973.

== Family ==
Her parents were George and Lillian Lyttle, both [[Jewish]].<ref name=JoanBirmanBio /> Her father was from Russia but grew up in [[Liverpool]], [[England]].  At age 17, George emigrated to the US and became a successful dress manufacturer. Her mother was born in New York and her parents were Russian-Polish immigrants.  

Birman's father appreciated the opportunities from having a business but he wanted his daughters to focus on education. 

Joan Birman married [[Joseph Birman]] in 1950, the year she and he gained Masters degrees in their respective fields.<ref name=JoanBirmanBio>{{cite web |url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Birman/ |title=Biography Joan Sylvia Lyttle Birman |first1=J J |last1=O’Connor |first2=E F |last2=Robertson |work=[[MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive]] |date=October 2015 |access-date=September 7, 2026 }}</ref> They have three children, [[Ken Birman|Kenneth Paul Birman]], Deborah Birman Shlider, and Carl David Birman. Her husband, who died in October 2016, was a physicist and a leading advocate for [[human rights]] for scientists.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/updates/josephbirman.cfm |title=Joseph L. Birman (1927–2016)|website=www.aps.org|access-date=2018-04-02}}{{dead link|date=September 2026}}</ref>

==Education==
After high school, Birman entered [[Swarthmore College]], a coeducational institution in Swarthmore, Pennsylvania, and majored in mathematics. However, she disliked living in the dorms so she transferred to [[Barnard College]], a women-only college affiliated with [[Columbia University]], in order to live at home.<ref name=JoanBirmanBio />

Birman received her B.A. in mathematics from Barnard College in 1948 and an M.A. in physics from Columbia University in 1950. After working in industry from 1950 to 1960, she studied mathematics at the [[Courant Institute]] at [[New York University]] under the supervision of [[Wilhelm Magnus]], earning her PhD in 1968. Her dissertation was titled "Braid groups and their relationship to mapping class groups".<ref name="MGP">{{MathGenealogy|id=24360|title=Joan Sylvia Lyttle Birman}}</ref>

==Career==
After she earned her bachelor's degree from Barnard, Birman accepted a position at the Polytechnic Research and Development Co., which was affiliated with [[New York University Tandon School of Engineering|Brooklyn Polytechnic University]]. She later worked for the Technical Research Group and the W. L. Maxson Corporation.<ref name=celebratio>{{cite web|title=Autobiography by Joan S. Birman|url=https://celebratio.org/Birman_JS/article/442/|website=Celbratio Mathematica|publisher=Mathematical Sciences Research Institute|access-date=20 February 2021}}</ref>

Birman's first academic position was at the [[Stevens Institute of Technology]] (1968–1973). When she joined, she was the only female professor of its 160-member faculty.<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 7, 2022 |title=Working at Their Full Potential: The Impact of the AMS Birman Fellowship |url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202203/rnoti-p452.pdf |access-date=October 20, 2022 |website=American Mathematical Society}}</ref>  In 1969 she published "On Braid Groups", which introduced a way to relate the [[mapping class group of a surface]] to the mapping class group of a punctured version of the same surface. Known as the Birman Exact Sequence, this has become one of the most important tools in the study of braids and surfaces.<ref name="notices">{{cite journal|author=Margalit, Dan|author-link=Dan Margalit (mathematician)|title=The Mathematics of Joan Birman|journal= AMS Notices |volume=66|issue=3|year=2019|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201903/rnoti-p341.pdf}}</ref> During the later part of this period, in 1974, she published a [[monograph]], ''[[Braids, Links, and Mapping Class Groups]]'', based on a graduate course she taught as a visiting professor at [[Princeton University]] in 1971–72. It is considered the first comprehensive treatment of braid theory. It introduced the modern theory to the field and offered the first complete proof of the [[Markov theorem]] on braids.<ref name="notices"/>

In 1973, she joined the faculty of Barnard College, where she served as chair of the Mathematics Department from 1973 to 1987, 1989 to 1991, and 1995 to 1998. She was a visiting scholar at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in the summer of 1988.<ref>[http://www.ias.edu/people/cos/ Institute for Advanced Study: A Community of Scholars]</ref>

She supervised 21 doctoral students, and has a total of 70 academic descendants. Her doctoral students include [[Józef Przytycki]] and [[Tara E. Brendle]].<ref name="MGP" />

Birman was a founding editor of the journals [[Geometry and Topology]] and [[Algebraic and Geometric Topology]].<ref name=amsinterview>{{cite journal |last1=Jackson |first1=Allyn |last2=Traynor |first2=Lisa |title=Interview with Joan Birman |journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society |date=January 2007 |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=20–29 |url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200701/fea-birman.pdf |access-date=20 February 2021}}</ref>

Birman was a co-founder of Mathematical Sciences Publishing, a non-profit publishing house. She was a member of the [[New York Academy of Sciences]] Human Rights of Scientists Committee.<ref name=essay>{{cite journal|last=Lam|first=Wai-TIng|title=The Charm of Topology Dr. Joan Birman: Mathematics is very beautiful|journal=Newsletter of the Association for Women in Mathematics|volume=39|issue=4|date=Jul–Aug 2009|pages=6–7}}</ref>

== Work ==
According to her MathSciNet author profile, Birman's scientific work includes 106 research publications and over 300 published reviews in Math Reviews. She is the author of the research monograph ''[[Braids, Links, and Mapping Class Groups]]''.

In 2026, Birman, with Vasudha Bharathram and [[Tara E. Brendle]] posted a proof of the faithfulness of the [[Burau representation]] when n = 4 to [[arXiv]], whose status had not previously been known.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Barber |first=Gregory |date=2026-09-06 |title=The 92-Year-Old Mathematician and the Teenage Apprentice |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/06/science/92-year-old-mathematician-apprentice.html |access-date=2026-09-06 |work=The New York Times |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

==Recognition==
In 1974, Birman was selected as a [[Sloan Fellows|Sloan Research Fellow]] by the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]].<ref name="sloan">{{cite web|title=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation Past Fellows|url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/joan-s-birman/ |publisher=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|access-date=September 7, 2026 |archive-date=14 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314000756/https://sloan.org/past-fellows|url-status=dead}}</ref> 

In 1994, she was selected as a [[Guggenheim Fellowship|Guggenheim Foundation Fellow]] by the [[John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation]].<ref name="guggenheim">{{cite web | title=Joan S. Birman | website=John Simon Guggenheim Foundation | url=https://www.gf.org/fellows/all-fellows/joan-s-birman/ | ref={{sfnref | John Simon Guggenheim Foundation}} | access-date=2021-02-20}}</ref> In 1996, the [[Mathematical Association of America]] awarded Birman the [[Chauvenet Prize]], "the highest award for mathematical [[expository writing]]" for her 1993 essay ''New Points of View in Knot Theory''.<ref>{{cite journal|author=Birman, Joan|title=New Points of View in Knot Theory|journal=Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. (N.S.)|volume=28|issue=2|year=1993|pages=253–287|url=http://www.maa.org/programs/maa-awards/writing-awards/new-points-of-view-in-knot-theory|doi=10.1090/s0273-0979-1993-00389-6|arxiv=math/9304209|bibcode=1993math......4209B|s2cid=17229952}}</ref> In 1997, Birman received an honorary doctorate from the [[Technion Israel Institute of Technology]].<ref name="amsinterview" />

In 2003, Birman was elected to the European Academy of Sciences.<ref name="euracad">{{cite web | title=Joan S. Birman | website=European Academy of Sciences | url=https://www.eurasc.org/user/220/joan-s-birman | ref={{sfnref | European Academy of Sciences}} | access-date=2021-02-20}}</ref> In 2005, she won the New York City Mayor's Award for Excellence in Science and Technology.<ref name="LRiddleBio" />

In 2012, Birman was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]<ref name="barnard">{{cite web | title=Prof. Joan S. Birman '48 elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences | website=Barnard College | date=2012-04-17 | url=https://barnard.edu/headlines/prof-joan-s-birman-48-elected-american-academy-arts-and-sciences | ref={{sfnref | Barnard College | 2012}} | access-date=2021-02-20}}</ref><ref name="aaas">{{cite web | title=Joan S. Lyttle Birman | website=American Academy of Arts & Sciences | date=2021-02-09 | url=https://www.amacad.org/person/joan-s-lyttle-birman | ref={{sfnref | American Academy of Arts & Sciences | 2021}} | access-date=2021-02-20}}</ref> In 2015, Birman was named an honorary member of the [[London Mathematical Society]].<ref name="lms">{{Cite journal|date=2016-03-28|title=Honorary Members 2015|journal=Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society|volume=48|issue=3|pages=548–556|doi=10.1112/blms/bdw014|s2cid=247694394 |issn=0024-6093}}</ref> In 2021, Birman was elected to the [[National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="nas">{{cite web|title=2021 NAS Election|url=http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210426172730/http://www.nasonline.org/news-and-multimedia/news/2021-nas-election.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=April 26, 2021|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=26 April 2021}}</ref>

=== American Mathematical Society ===
From 1978 to 1980, and again from 1990 to 1992, Birman was an [[American Mathematical Society]] (AMS) Council member at large.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AMS Committees |url=http://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |access-date=2023-03-27 |website=American Mathematical Society |language=en}}</ref> 

In 1990, Birman donated funds to the AMS to establish the [[Ruth Lyttle Satter Prize in Mathematics]] in honor of her sister, [[Ruth Lyttle Satter]], who was a [[plant physiologist]].<ref name="amsinterview" /> In 2017, she endowed the Joan and Joseph Birman Fellowship for Women Scholars at the AMS to support mathematical research by mid-career women.<ref>{{Cite web |title=American Mathematical Society – The Joan and Joseph Birman Fellowship for Women Scholars |url=https://www.ams.org/programs/ams-fellowships/Birman-fellow |access-date=2018-04-02 |website=www.ams.org}}</ref>

In 2013, she became a fellow of the American Mathematical Society in the inaugural class.<ref>[https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2012-11-10.</ref>

=== Association of Women in Mathematics ===
In 1987, she was selected by the [[Association for Women in Mathematics]] to be a [[Noether Lecturer]], honoring her fundamental and sustained contributions to the mathematical sciences.<ref>{{cite web |title=Noether Lectures 1987 Lecturer: Joan S. Birman |url=https://awm-math.org/awards/noether-lectures/noether-lectures-1987/ |access-date=10 April 2021 |website=Association for Women in Mathematics}}</ref>

In 2015, the Association for Women in Mathematics began awarding the Joan & Joseph Birman Research Prize in Topology and Geometry.<ref name="AWM Birman Research Prize">{{cite web |title=AWM Birman Research Prize |url=https://awm-math.org/awards/awm-birman-research-prize/ |access-date=2022-12-01 |website=Association for Women in Mathematics (AWM)}}</ref> In 2020, they included her in that year's class of Fellows for "her groundbreaking research connecting diverse fields, and for her award-winning expository writing; for continuously supporting women in mathematics as an active mentor and a research role model; and for sponsoring multiple prize initiatives for women".<ref>{{citation |title=2020 Class of AWM Fellows |url=https://awm-math.org/awards/awm-fellows/2020-awm-fellows/ |access-date=2019-11-08 |publisher=[[Association for Women in Mathematics]]}}</ref> The AWM also included her in a deck of cards featuring notable women mathematicians.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mathematicians of EvenQuads Deck 1 |url=https://awm-math.org/publications/playing-cards/deck1/#birman |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=awm-math.org}}</ref>
